shape.subject: Additional Mathematics
shape.scope: Quadratic functions, equations and inequalities (incl. nature of roots, simultaneous equations involving one linear and one non-linear equation); surds; indices and logarithms (incl. exponential growth/decay models); polynomials, remainder and factor theorems, partial fractions; binomial theorem for positive integer index; linear law; coordinate geometry of straight lines, perpendicular bisectors, areas of rectilinear figures; equations of circles; plane geometry proofs (angle properties of circles, similar/congruent triangles, tangent-chord theorem, midpoint theorem, intersecting chords); trigonometry (ratios of special angles, graphs of sin/cos/tan and their transformations, identities incl. sec/cosec/cot, addition and double-angle formulae, R-formula, equations, real-world models); differentiation (chain/product/quotient rules, trig/exp/log functions, tangents and normals, increasing/decreasing functions, rates of change, maxima/minima); integration (as reverse of differentiation, standard forms incl. (ax+b)^n, trig, e^x, 1/x, definite integrals, areas between curves and lines); kinematics of a particle in a straight line via calculus. NOT in 4049: vectors, matrices, statistics, complex numbers, integration by parts or substitution, inverse trigonometric functions, series beyond binomial.
shape.register:
REGISTER — how SEAB asks
- Plain, exact, economical English. Instructions are imperatives: Find, Show that, Hence, Explain why, Determine, Express, Solve, Sketch, State, Calculate, Verify, Use … to …, Given that …
- Parts are labelled (a), (b), (c), with sub-parts (i), (ii). Every part carries its marks. A single-part question has no labels.
- Precision demands are explicit: "giving your answer in the form $a + b\sqrt{3}$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers", "correct to 2 decimal places", "in terms of $\pi$", "in exact form", "in logarithmic form".
- A "Show that"/"Prove that" part states its target exactly; a later part uses it ("Hence …", "Using your answer to part (a) …").
- Contexts are brief and concrete (a coffee machine, a patch of water, a ball thrown upwards), never chatty; units are given; constants are named ("where $k$ is a constant"); the model is stated as a formula.
- "A calculator must not be used in this question." opens a question whose point is exact arithmetic (surds, exact trigonometric values). Otherwise no calculator remark.
- Function notation $\mathrm{f}(x)$, $\mathrm{f}'(x)$, $\frac{dy}{dx}$, $\int \ldots \,dx$; angles in radians unless degrees are stated; a domain such as $0 \le x \le 2\pi$ or $-\frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}$ is always stated for a trigonometric equation.
- Marks follow the work: about 1 mark per 1.5 minutes. 1–2 marks: state/verify/one-line deduction. 3–4 marks: one standard routine. 5–7 marks: a multi-step argument. A long closing question of 9–12 marks has 3–5 parts that build on one another.

title: A Math · Set 2 · Paper 1 · O-Level format

question.stem: It is given that $\mathrm{f}(x) = (k - 2)x^2 + (4k - 8)x + 3k - 1$. Find the set of values of the constant $k$ for which $\mathrm{f}(x) > 0$ for all real values of $x$.
skills: condition for a quadratic expression to be positive for all real x: positive leading coefficient and negative discriminant, solved as a factorised quadratic inequality in k
noticing that the leading coefficient itself can vanish and checking that case separately: at k = 2 f(x) is the constant 5, so k = 2 is kept
excluding the strict end point k = 7, where f(x) becomes the perfect square 5(x + 2)^2 and equals 0 at x = -2
question.solution:
Case $k = 2$: $\mathrm{f}(x) = 0x^2 + 0x + 3(2) - 1 = 5$, and $5 > 0$ for all real $x$. So $k = 2$ satisfies the condition (the discriminant method does not apply here, because $\mathrm{f}$ is not a quadratic). [B1, a separate mark that can be earned by itself]

Case $k \ne 2$: $\mathrm{f}(x)$ is a quadratic in $x$, and $\mathrm{f}(x) > 0$ for all real $x$ requires the coefficient of $x^2$ to be positive and the discriminant to be negative.
Coefficient of $x^2$: $k - 2 > 0$, so $k > 2$. (For $k < 2$ the coefficient of $x^2$ is negative, so $\mathrm{f}(x) < 0$ for large $|x|$ and every $k < 2$ fails.)
Discriminant: $(4k - 8)^2 - 4(k - 2)(3k - 1) = 16(k - 2)^2 - 4(k - 2)(3k - 1)$ [M1 for the two conditions $k - 2 > 0$ and discriminant $< 0$, with the discriminant formed]
$= 4(k - 2)\left[4(k - 2) - (3k - 1)\right] = 4(k - 2)(k - 7)$ [M1]
(or expanded: $16k^2 - 64k + 64 - 12k^2 + 28k - 8 = 4k^2 - 36k + 56 = 4(k - 2)(k - 7)$).
$4(k - 2)(k - 7) < 0 \Rightarrow 2 < k < 7$, which also satisfies $k > 2$.
Check of the end point $k = 7$: $\mathrm{f}(x) = 5x^2 + 20x + 20 = 5(x + 2)^2$, which equals $0$ at $x = -2$, so $k = 7$ is excluded. [A1 for $2 < k < 7$, with $k = 7$ excluded]

Combining the two cases: $2 \le k < 7$.

Alternative route: $\mathrm{f}(x) = (k - 2)(x + 2)^2 + 7 - k$. For $k > 2$ the least value is $7 - k$, which is positive when $k < 7$; for $k < 2$ the curve opens downwards and $\mathrm{f}(x)$ becomes negative for large $|x|$; for $k = 2$, $\mathrm{f}(x) = 5$. Hence $2 \le k < 7$.

Mark scheme: B1 $k = 2$ kept because $\mathrm{f}(x) = 5 > 0$ (a separate mark, earned by itself); M1 the two conditions for $k \ne 2$ set up with the discriminant formed (the line that every $k < 2$ fails because the leading coefficient is negative earns its credit inside this M1 and is not to be skipped); M1 the discriminant factorised or solved to $2 < k < 7$; A1 $2 < k < 7$ for the quadratic case, with $k = 7$ excluded. The answer $2 \le k < 7$ scores 4/4. The answer $2 < k < 7$ (forgetting that $k = 2$ makes $\mathrm{f}$ the constant $5$) scores 3/4 (B0), and $2 \le k \le 7$ (keeping the perfect square) scores 3/4 (A0).
question.syllabus_check: 4049 Quadratic functions: conditions for a quadratic expression to be always positive (sign of the leading coefficient and of the discriminant), solving a quadratic inequality, completing the square. The case where the coefficient of x^2 vanishes is checked by direct substitution only. No sum/product of roots, nothing outside 4049.
question.originality_note: Not a re-skin of GCE 2025 P1 Q2 (a curve completely below a line: subtract the line, two conditions, reject the branch k > 1/2) or GCE 2023 P1 Q7 (curve below the x-axis): there is no line, no branch to reject, and the idea is that the leading coefficient k - 2 can itself be zero, a case the discriminant method silently drops and that must be KEPT, while the other end point k = 7 (a perfect square touching zero) is excluded. Differs from Set 1 P1 Q1 (vertex by completing the square placed on a line) and Set 1 P1 Q4 (distance inequality and least distance); Set 1 P2 Q5(b) used a discriminant only to show no stationary points. Unparted, as the paper plan asks.

answers.single: {k : 2 ≤ k < 7}  (k = 2 gives f(x) = 5 > 0 for all x; for k ≠ 2 need k − 2 > 0 and discriminant 4(k − 2)(k − 7) < 0, giving 2 < k < 7)

issues: Degenerate case: at k = 2 the x^2 and x coefficients both vanish and f(x) = 5 > 0 for all real x, so k = 2 belongs in the set. The full answer is 2 ≤ k < 7, not 2 < k < 7. The mark scheme must accept/require k = 2, or the question should restrict k ≠ 2 (or say f is a quadratic) if 2 < k < 7 is the intended answer.

parts.label: single
parts.note: Setter 2 <= k < 7; blind examiner {k : 2 <= k < 7}. Checked independently: f(x) = (k - 2)(x + 2)^2 + 7 - k and the discriminant is 4(k - 2)(k - 7). For k < 2 the leading coefficient is negative, so f fails. At k = 2, f(x) = 5 > 0, so k = 2 is kept. For 2 < k < 7 the least value 7 - k is positive. At k = 7, f(x) = 5(x + 2)^2 = 0 at x = -2, so k = 7 is excluded. The blind examiner's 'issue' only asks the mark scheme to require k = 2, and the setter's scheme already does that (B1, and the A1 is lost for 2 < k < 7).

verdict.key_verdict: Both are right. The answer 2 <= k < 7 is correct at both ends: k = 2 makes f the constant 5, and k = 7 makes f a perfect square that reaches 0.
fixes: Light register edit: follow GCE 2025 P1 Q2 and put the constant in the command, e.g. 'It is given that f(x) = (k - 2)x^2 + (4k - 8)x + 3k - 1. Find the set of values of the constant k for which f(x) > 0 for all real values of x.' Keep f given directly. Do NOT recast it as a curve lying above a line, because that would be a re-skin of GCE 2025 P1 Q2. Do NOT add 'quadratic' to the stem, because the question's one idea is that f need not be a quadratic.

Mark scheme: keep 'k = 2 gives f(x) = 5 > 0' as a separate B1 so that it can be earned by itself, and state that both 2 < k < 7 and 2 <= k <= 7 score 3/4. The line saying that k < 2 fails because the leading coefficient is negative should earn credit inside M1, not be skipped.
verdict.why: This is a clean 4-mark opener any candidate can start, with one idea: the leading coefficient k - 2 can vanish, and that case must be KEPT. The engineering is neat, because k = 2 is also where the discriminant's factor vanishes, so the A1 is 'one end in, one out'. That is exactly the quality standard.md §6.6 praises in Set 1 P1 Q2(b), and it is more demanding than Set 1 P1 Q1 at the same marks. It is not a re-skin. GCE 2025 P1 Q2 uses the same syllabus technique but has no line to subtract, and there the twist REJECTS a branch rather than keeping a degenerate case. Set 1 P2 Q5(b) used a monic discriminant with no leading-coefficient condition. It scores 4, not 5, because an A1 that hangs on the degenerate case has more of the flavour of a top-school prelim than of SEAB, and the wording wants the light edit above.

question.stem: The equation of a curve is $y = \ln\left(x + \sqrt{x^2 + a^2}\right)$, where $a$ is a positive constant.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find $\frac{dy}{dx}$, giving your answer in its simplest form.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find, in terms of $a$, the $x$-coordinates of the points on the curve at which the gradient is half the gradient at the point where the curve crosses the $y$-axis.

skills: chain rule on $\ln$ of $x + \sqrt{x^2 + a^2}$, simplified by seeing that the derivative's numerator is the logarithm's own argument, to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 + a^2}}$
working back from a gradient condition stated relative to the $y$-intercept to the $x$-coordinates in terms of a general constant $a$
both roots of $x^2 = 3a^2$ stand: $x = \sqrt{3}\,a$ and $x = -\sqrt{3}\,a$, with no root rejected
question.solution:
(a) Let $u = x + \sqrt{x^2 + a^2}$, so $y = \ln u$ and $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{u}\frac{du}{dx}$.
$\frac{du}{dx} = 1 + \frac{1}{2}\left(x^2 + a^2\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}(2x) = 1 + \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + a^2}} = \frac{\sqrt{x^2 + a^2} + x}{\sqrt{x^2 + a^2}}$  [M1 for the chain rule on the root]
$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\sqrt{x^2 + a^2} + x}{\sqrt{x^2 + a^2}\left(x + \sqrt{x^2 + a^2}\right)}$  [M1 for $\frac{u'}{u}$]
The numerator is the same as the bracket $x + \sqrt{x^2 + a^2}$ in the denominator, so it cancels:
$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 + a^2}}$  [A1]

(b) The curve crosses the $y$-axis where $x = 0$ (at $(0, \ln a)$). There the gradient is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{a^2}} = \frac{1}{a}$, since $a > 0$.
Half of this gradient is $\frac{1}{2a}$, so
$\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 + a^2}} = \frac{1}{2a}$
$\sqrt{x^2 + a^2} = 2a$
$x^2 + a^2 = 4a^2$
$x^2 = 3a^2$  [M1 for the equation and solving to $x^2 = 3a^2$]
$x = \sqrt{3}\,a$ or $x = -\sqrt{3}\,a$.
Both values are kept: for every real $x$, $\sqrt{x^2 + a^2} > |x|$, so $x + \sqrt{x^2 + a^2} > 0$ and the curve exists there. At these points $x + \sqrt{x^2 + a^2} = (2 \pm \sqrt{3})a > 0$.
$x = \sqrt{3}\,a$ or $x = -\sqrt{3}\,a$  [A1 for both; A0 if $-\sqrt{3}\,a$ is rejected]
question.syllabus_check: 4049 differentiation: derivative of $\ln x$ and of powers, the chain rule for composite functions, simplification of the result; solving an equation involving a square root by squaring. No inverse hyperbolic or inverse trigonometric knowledge is needed: the curve is differentiated purely by the chain rule. No integration, no implicit differentiation.
question.originality_note: The curve $y = \ln\left(x + \sqrt{x^2 + a^2}\right)$ appears in no GCE paper in the corpus and in no earlier Set. Unlike GCE 2024 P1 Q2 (differentiate $\sqrt{x^2 + x + 1}$, then hence integrate), GCE 2021 P2 Q3 and GCE 2025 P1 Q4 (printed or general derivative, then an integral) and Set 1 P2 Q3 and Q5 (product rules with a printed derivative, then reverse integration), this question has no integral and no printed target: the candidate must see the collapse to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 + a^2}}$ unaided, then work back from a gradient condition to $x$ in terms of the general constant $a$, where both roots $\pm\sqrt{3}a$ stand. Set 1's stationary-point condition in $k$ (P2 Q5) is not used: nothing here is stationary.

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both give dy/dx = 1/√(x² + a²). Checked: u = x + √(x²+a²), u' = (√(x²+a²) + x)/√(x²+a²), and u'/u cancels to 1/√(x²+a²).

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both give x = ±√3 a. Checked: the gradient at x = 0 is 1/a (a > 0). Setting 1/√(x²+a²) = 1/(2a) gives x² = 3a². At x = −√3 a the argument is (2 − √3)a > 0, so both roots stand.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter and the blind examiner agree on both parts, and I worked both parts myself: the key is right.
fixes: Put (b) into SEAB's register: "Find, in terms of $a$, the $x$-coordinates of the points on the curve at which the gradient is half the gradient at the point where the curve crosses the $y$-axis." This replaces 'the values of x at which' and 'half of the gradient'.

The third skill phrase oversells the decision in (b). The gradient function 1/√(x²+a²) is even, so ±√3 a comes out by symmetry and almost no candidate will be tempted to reject −√3 a. Reword the phrase to say only that both roots of x² = 3a² stand. Or, optionally, give (b) a real boundary: ask for the set of values of x for which the gradient is LESS than half the gradient at the y-axis crossing. The A1 is then the two-sided set x < −√3 a or x > √3 a, at the same [2].
verdict.why: This is a clean question at the 2024/25 standard for 5 marks. The form of the derivative is not printed, so in (a) the candidate has to see that the numerator is the logarithm's own argument and cancel it (the 2025 'target no longer printed' trait). The unprinted simplified form feeds (b), and the constant a is carried to an unprinted answer. It is harder than GCE 2024 P1 Q2 or GCE 2025 P1 Q4(a) and not a re-skin of either. It also differs from Set 1 P2 Q3 and Q5, which used the product rule, a printed derivative and a reverse integral. It sits well beside Set 1 P1 Q1–Q3. The only weak point is that (b) is thin: gradient at x = 0, halve it, solve. Its 'kept negative root' is a mild trap, not a real decision.

question.stem: Do not use a calculator in this question.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Express $\sin\theta\cos\theta\cos 2\theta\cos 4\theta$ in the form $k\sin n\theta$, where $k$ is a constant and $n$ is a positive integer.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Hence find the exact value of $\cos\frac{\pi}{7}\cos\frac{2\pi}{7}\cos\frac{4\pi}{7}$.

skills: double-angle formula used backwards three times to collapse a product of cosines into $k\sin n\theta$
evaluating a product of cosines of non-special angles exactly by bringing in the missing factor $\sin\frac{\pi}{7}$
sign of $\sin\frac{8\pi}{7}$ from its basic angle, giving a negative exact value
question.solution:
(a) Use $\sin 2A = 2\sin A\cos A$ backwards, three times.
$\sin\theta\cos\theta = \frac{1}{2}\sin 2\theta$
So $\sin\theta\cos\theta\cos 2\theta\cos 4\theta = \frac{1}{2}\sin 2\theta\cos 2\theta\cos 4\theta$  [M1]
$= \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\sin 4\theta\cos 4\theta = \frac{1}{4}\sin 4\theta\cos 4\theta$
$= \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\sin 8\theta = \frac{1}{8}\sin 8\theta$
So $k = \frac{1}{8}$ and $n = 8$.  [A1]

(b) The product asked for is the expression of part (a) at $\theta = \frac{\pi}{7}$ without its factor $\sin\theta$, so put $\theta = \frac{\pi}{7}$ in part (a):
$\sin\frac{\pi}{7}\cos\frac{\pi}{7}\cos\frac{2\pi}{7}\cos\frac{4\pi}{7} = \frac{1}{8}\sin\frac{8\pi}{7}$  [M1]
$\frac{8\pi}{7} = \pi + \frac{\pi}{7}$ lies in the third quadrant, where sine is negative, with basic angle $\frac{\pi}{7}$:
$\sin\frac{8\pi}{7} = -\sin\frac{\pi}{7}$  [M1, the related-angle step on which the A1 rests]
So $\sin\frac{\pi}{7}\cos\frac{\pi}{7}\cos\frac{2\pi}{7}\cos\frac{4\pi}{7} = -\frac{1}{8}\sin\frac{\pi}{7}$.
Since $0 < \frac{\pi}{7} < \pi$, $\sin\frac{\pi}{7} \ne 0$, so divide both sides by $\sin\frac{\pi}{7}$:
$\cos\frac{\pi}{7}\cos\frac{2\pi}{7}\cos\frac{4\pi}{7} = -\frac{1}{8}$  [A1]
Check of sign: $\frac{\pi}{7}$ and $\frac{2\pi}{7}$ are acute, so their cosines are positive, while $\frac{\pi}{2} < \frac{4\pi}{7} < \pi$, so $\cos\frac{4\pi}{7} < 0$; the product must be negative. (Numerically $0.9010 \times 0.6235 \times (-0.2225) = -0.1250$.)
Mark scheme for (b): first M1 for $\theta = \frac{\pi}{7}$ in part (a), or for the equivalent route that multiplies the product by $\sin\frac{\pi}{7}$ and folds it up with the double-angle formula to $\frac{1}{8}\sin\frac{8\pi}{7}$; second M1 for the related-angle step $\sin\frac{8\pi}{7} = -\sin\frac{\pi}{7}$; A1 $-\frac{1}{8}$, which rests on that step.
Common errors: taking $\sin\frac{8\pi}{7} = \sin\frac{\pi}{7}$ and giving $\frac{1}{8}$ (M1 M0 A0); substituting $\theta = \frac{\pi}{7}$ but not dividing by $\sin\frac{\pi}{7}$ (M1 only).
question.syllabus_check: 4049 trigonometry only: the double-angle formula $\sin 2A = 2\sin A\cos A$ (used in reverse), trigonometric ratios of a general angle in radians (related angle and the sign of sine in the third quadrant), and exact values without a calculator. No factor (sum-to-product) formulae, no inverse trigonometric functions, nothing outside the syllabus is needed; (a) is an identity valid for all $\theta$, so no domain is required.
question.originality_note: No GCE question in the corpus and no earlier Set collapses a product of cosines by repeated use of the double-angle formula. The nearest real items (GCE 2023 P2 Q4 and GCE 2022 P2 Q5, tan 15 and tan 75 degrees from tan 2A; GCE 2021 specimen P1 Q8, cos 75 degrees and sec squared 75 degrees) find a surd value for a SPECIAL angle; here the angles pi/7, 2pi/7 and 4pi/7 are not special, the answer is rational, and the A1 hangs on the sign of sin(8pi/7). It differs from Set 1 P1 Q3, which proved a compound-angle product identity and the triple-angle formula as two unrelated printed proofs: here the double-angle formula is used backwards to an UNPRINTED form, and part (b) evaluates rather than proves, depending on part (a).

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both give (1/8) sin 8θ, k = 1/8, n = 8. Checked: sinθcosθ = ½ sin2θ, then ¼ sin4θ, then ⅛ sin8θ; numerically identical at θ = 0.3, 1.1, 2.5. The form is unique because n is a positive integer.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on both parts, and the key is right: (a) (1/8) sin 8θ, (b) −1/8.
fixes: Register (light edit): head the question in SEAB's current wording, 'Do not use a calculator in this question.' (as in GCE 2025 P2 Q4), or open (b) with 'Without using a calculator,' (as in GCE 2024 P1 Q7). This is optional: Set 1 P1 Q8 used the present wording and was approved.

Mark scheme for (b): award the first M1 for the equivalent route that multiplies the product by sin(π/7) and folds it up with the double-angle formula. Make the second M1 explicitly the related-angle step sin(8π/7) = −sin(π/7), which the A1 rests on, so that a candidate answering +1/8 scores M1 M0 A0.
Keep π/7 and do not swap it for π/9: with π/9, sin(8π/9) = +sin(π/9), the sign trap disappears and (b) drops to routine.
verdict.why: (a) is an honest 2-mark routine. The idea sits in (b) [3]: the candidate must see that the product is (a) at θ = π/7 without the factor sin(π/7), then cancel it through sin(8π/7) = −sin(π/7), with the A1 depending on the negative sign. That is exactly the §2 3-mark band of one decision followed by a short routine. It re-skins no 2024/25 question and no earlier Set question (Set 1 P1 Q3 had two unrelated printed proofs of compound-angle and triple-angle identities). It also does better than that Set 1 question of the same marks, because its parts build on each other and no target is printed.

question.stem: A trough of length $200$ cm has a uniform cross-section in the shape of an isosceles trapezium. The trough stands on horizontal ground with its shorter parallel side as its base, and it has negligible thickness. The base of the trough is $30$ cm wide, the open top is $90$ cm wide and the trough is $40$ cm deep. The trough is initially empty. Water is poured into it at a constant rate of $36\,000$ cm$^3$ per minute. Find the rate at which the depth of the water is increasing $5$ minutes after the water starts to flow.
skills: express the water-surface width in a trough of trapezium cross-section as a linear function of the depth and build the volume of water
find the depth at a given elapsed time from the volume poured, solving a quadratic and rejecting the negative root
connected rates dh/dt = (dV/dt)/(dV/dh) for a constant inflow into a non-uniform cross-section
question.solution:
Let the depth of the water be $h$ cm and its volume $V$ cm$^3$ at time $t$ minutes.
Each sloping side moves out $\frac{90 - 30}{2} = 30$ cm horizontally over the full depth of $40$ cm, so at height $h$ above the bottom it has moved out $\frac{30}{40}h = \frac{3}{4}h$ cm (similar triangles).
Width of the water surface $= 30 + 2\left(\frac{3}{4}h\right) = 30 + \frac{3}{2}h$.
Area of the cross-section of the water $= \frac{1}{2}\left(30 + 30 + \frac{3}{2}h\right)h = 30h + \frac{3}{4}h^2$.
$V = 200\left(30h + \frac{3}{4}h^2\right) = 6000h + 150h^2$.
After $5$ minutes, $V = 36\,000 \times 5 = 180\,000$.
$150h^2 + 6000h = 180\,000 \Rightarrow h^2 + 40h - 1200 = 0 \Rightarrow (h - 20)(h + 60) = 0$.
$h = 20$ ($h = -60$ is rejected since a depth cannot be negative; $20 < 40$, so the trough has not overflowed).
$\frac{dV}{dh} = 6000 + 300h = 12\,000$ when $h = 20$.
$\frac{dh}{dt} = \frac{dV}{dt} \div \frac{dV}{dh} = \frac{36\,000}{12\,000} = 3$.
The depth of the water is increasing at $3$ cm per minute.
Mark scheme: M1 width of the water surface $30 + \frac{3}{2}h$ (or the overhang $\frac{3}{4}h$ on each side); M1 $V = 6000h + 150h^2$ (any equivalent form, e.g. $150h(h + 40)$); M1 $V = 180\,000$ and the quadratic in $h$; A1 $h = 20$ with $-60$ rejected; M1 $\frac{dV}{dh} = 6000 + 300h$ used in $\frac{dh}{dt} = \frac{dV}{dt} \div \frac{dV}{dh}$; A1 $3$ cm per minute.
question.syllabus_check: 4049 Differentiation: rates of change by the chain rule ($\frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{dV}{dh} \times \frac{dh}{dt}$). Uses only assumed knowledge: area of a trapezium, volume of a prism, similar triangles or a constant slope, and solving a quadratic equation. No formula is printed; nothing outside 4049.
question.originality_note: Not in the SEAB 2019-2025 corpus or in Set 1. Set 1 P1 Q11 (folding fan) differentiates a chord and a triangle area with respect to an angle; GCE 2025 P1 Q11 builds a hypotenuse by Pythagoras for a moving point; GCE 2024 P1 Q1 and GCE 2023 P1 Q11 are circle areas; GCE 2020 P2 Q11 (cone) and GCE 2018 P1 Q7 (bowl) print the volume formula. Here nothing is printed: the candidate must see that the water surface widens linearly with depth (3 cm across for every 4 cm up on each side), build the volume $150h(h + 40)$, and, because the instant is given as an elapsed time rather than a depth, first find the depth from the volume poured by solving a quadratic and rejecting $h = -60$. A trough of trapezium section is a familiar textbook setting; the elapsed-time instant, the 3:4 side slope and all numbers are new.

parts.label: single
parts.note: Setter and blind examiner both give 3 cm per minute. Checked independently: overhang 3/4 cm per cm of depth, V = 6000h + 150h^2, V(5 min) = 180 000 gives h^2 + 40h - 1200 = 0, h = 20 (-60 rejected; 20 < 40 and 180 000 < the full 480 000, so no overflow), dV/dh = 12 000, dh/dt = 36 000/12 000 = 3.

verdict.key_verdict: No disagreement: the key of 3 cm per minute is correct, and the discriminant is a perfect square so every step closes exactly.
fixes: Light edit to SEAB's register: 'A trough of length 200 cm has a uniform cross-section in the shape of an isosceles trapezium. The trough stands on horizontal ground with its shorter parallel side as its base. The base of the trough is 30 cm wide, the open top is 90 cm wide and the trough is 40 cm deep.' This drops the laboured 'is a prism ... whose parallel sides are horizontal' while keeping what defines the depth.
State that the trough has negligible thickness, or that the dimensions are internal, so that 30, 90 and 40 are unambiguously the dimensions of the water space.

Keep the question unparted. The slot plan said 2 parts, but splitting this model into [4] + [2] (for example 'show that V = 6000h + 150h^2') is the item-12 anti-pattern and would print the relation the question exists to test. The paper also needs unparted models (List B 3b).

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Solve the equation $\tan 2x = 2\cos x$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Hence solve the equation $\cot 2x = \frac{1}{2}\sec x$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$.

skills: factorise out cos x instead of dividing by it, keeping the solution where both sides of tan 2x = 2cos x are zero
choose cos 2x = 1 - 2sin^2 x so the remaining factor becomes a quadratic in sin x
reject the solutions at which the reciprocal equation cot 2x = (1/2)sec x is undefined
question.solution:
(a) Write $\tan 2x = \frac{\sin 2x}{\cos 2x}$, where $\cos 2x \ne 0$, and $\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x$:
$\frac{2\sin x\cos x}{\cos 2x} = 2\cos x$
$2\sin x\cos x = 2\cos x\cos 2x$ [M1]
Bring everything to one side and factorise (do NOT divide by $\cos x$):
$2\cos x\cos 2x - 2\sin x\cos x = 0$
$2\cos x\,(\cos 2x - \sin x) = 0$ [M1]
So $\cos x = 0$ or $\cos 2x = \sin x$.
For the second factor use $\cos 2x = 1 - 2\sin^2 x$:
$1 - 2\sin^2 x - \sin x = 0$
$2\sin^2 x + \sin x - 1 = 0$ [M1]
$(2\sin x - 1)(\sin x + 1) = 0$ [M1]
$\cos x = 0$: $x = 90^\circ$ or $x = 270^\circ$.
$\sin x = \frac{1}{2}$: $x = 30^\circ$ or $x = 150^\circ$.
$\sin x = -1$: $x = 270^\circ$ (already found).
Check that $\tan 2x$ is defined at each value: $\cos 2x = \frac{1}{2}, -1, \frac{1}{2}, -1$ at $x = 30^\circ, 90^\circ, 150^\circ, 270^\circ$, never $0$.
$x = 30^\circ, 90^\circ, 150^\circ, 270^\circ$ [A1]
Note: at $x = 90^\circ$, $\tan 180^\circ = 0 = 2\cos 90^\circ$, so $90^\circ$ is a solution. A candidate who divides by $\cos x$, or who writes $\tan 2x = \frac{2\tan x}{1 - \tan^2 x}$ (undefined at $x = 90^\circ$), loses $x = 90^\circ$; $270^\circ$ survives that error only because it also comes from $\sin x = -1$. The A1 requires all four values and no others.

(b) $\cot 2x = \frac{1}{2}\sec x$ means $\frac{1}{\tan 2x} = \frac{1}{2\cos x}$, the equation of part (a) turned upside down. It needs $\sec x$ to be defined, so $\cos x \ne 0$; and since $\frac{1}{2}\sec x$ is never zero, $\cot 2x \ne 0$ at a solution, so $\tan 2x$ is defined and non-zero. Under these conditions the equation is equivalent to $\tan 2x = 2\cos x$. [M1]
So its solutions are the solutions of part (a) at which $\cos x \ne 0$. At $x = 90^\circ$ and $x = 270^\circ$, $\cos x = 0$: $\sec x$ is undefined (and so is $\cot 180^\circ$, $\cot 540^\circ$), so both are rejected.
$x = 30^\circ, 150^\circ$ [A1]
Check: $\cot 60^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ and $\frac{1}{2}\sec 30^\circ = \frac{1}{2}\times\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$; $\cot 300^\circ = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ and $\frac{1}{2}\sec 150^\circ = \frac{1}{2}\times\left(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.
Solving (b) directly gives $2\cos x(\cos 2x - \sin x) = 0$ again; $\cos x = 0$ is now rejected, and so is $\sin x = -1$, since it gives $x = 270^\circ$ where $\cos x = 0$. The A1 requires $30^\circ$ and $150^\circ$ only.
question.syllabus_check: 4049 Trigonometry: double-angle formulae for sin 2A, cos 2A and tan 2A; the reciprocal functions sec and cot; solving a trigonometric equation in a stated interval in degrees, including the factorised form and the values at which a function is undefined. No R-formula, no binomial, no general solutions, no calculator values needed.
question.originality_note: Not a prove-then-hence-solve and no printed target: (a) is a bare equation whose A1 hangs on KEEPING the cos x = 0 case (dividing by cos x, or using tan 2x = 2tan x/(1 - tan^2 x), silently loses 90 degrees while 270 degrees survives through sin x = -1, so the loss is easy to miss); (b) takes the reciprocal of the same equation, so exactly the kept solutions must now be REJECTED. Set 1's trigonometric equations were a tan quartic from a binomial difference (kept theta = 0, rejected tan^2 theta = -41), an R-form equation answered in terms of pi, and a cosine pedal model; none factorises out cos x, uses a double angle as the route to a quadratic in sin x, or contrasts a kept case with the same case rejected. Nearest real question GCE 2022 P2 Q3 proves the identity tan 2theta(2cos theta - sec theta) = 2 sin theta and then solves; this question proves nothing, and its equation, answers and second part are different.

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both give x = 30°, 90°, 150°, 270°. Checked: 2 sin x cos x = 2 cos x cos 2x gives cos x (cos 2x − sin x) = 0; cos x = 0 gives 90° and 270°, where tan 180° = tan 540° = 0 = 2 cos x; 2sin²x + sin x − 1 = (2 sin x − 1)(sin x + 1) = 0 gives 30°, 150° and 270° again. cos 2x ≠ 0 at every root (1/2, −1, 1/2, −1), and cross-multiplying adds no false root (at x = 45°, 135°, 225°, 315° the product form fails). x = 0° and 360° are not solutions.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both give x = 30°, 150°. Checked directly: cos 2x / sin 2x = 1/(2 cos x) needs cos x ≠ 0 and sin 2x ≠ 0, and gives cos x (cos 2x − sin x) = 0 again. Every cos x = 0 root is rejected, and so is sin x = −1 (270°). Also ½ sec x is never 0, so a point where tan 2x is undefined cannot be a root. cot 60° = 1/√3 = ½ sec 30°, and cot 300° = −1/√3 = ½ sec 150°.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter's key and the blind examiner agree on both parts, and my own working gives the same answers: (a) 30°, 90°, 150°, 270°; (b) 30°, 150°.
verdict.why: (a) is an unscaffolded [5] chain whose A1 depends on KEEPING x = 90°. Both sides are zero there, so a candidate who divides by cos x, or who uses tan 2x = 2tan x/(1 − tan²x), loses it. 270° survives that error only because sin x = −1 also gives it. (b) is a 2-mark consequence that must be read exactly: the same cases are now REJECTED. That is the case-kept and case-rejected A1 of the 2024/25 standard (§6.6), with clean special-angle answers. It is as demanding for its marks as GCE 2025 P1 Q9 [4, 3] and Set 1 P1 Q5 [7], and it prints no target. It is not a re-skin. GCE 2022 P2 Q3 has the same ingredients (tan 2θ, 2cos θ, ½ sec θ), but it is a prove-then-hence-solve with a different equation and different answers. No earlier Set asked a double-angle equation that needs a factorised case kept and then rejected. The skills phrases are true and specific. All gates passed.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find $\int \mathrm{f}(x)\,dx$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Hence find the value of the constant $k$, where $k > 1$, for which $\int_{1}^{k} \mathrm{f}(x)\,dx = 0$.

skills: split a quotient over $\sqrt{x}$ into powers of $x$ before integrating
set a definite integral with an unknown upper limit equal to zero and recognise the result as a cubic in $\sqrt{k}$

factorise the cubic in $\sqrt{k}$ from the root $\sqrt{k} = 1$ given by the lower limit; reject $\sqrt{k} = -5$ because a square root cannot be negative (squaring it gives the false $k = 25$), and $\sqrt{k} = 1$ by $k > 1$
question.solution:
(a) $\mathrm{f}(x) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x}} - \frac{7}{\sqrt{x}} = x^{\frac{1}{2}} - 7x^{-\frac{1}{2}}$.   [M1: fraction split into powers of $x$]
$\int \mathrm{f}(x)\,dx = \frac{x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}} - \frac{7x^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\frac{1}{2}} + c = \frac{2}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}} - 14x^{\frac{1}{2}} + c$.   [A1]

(b) Using (a), $\int_{1}^{k} \mathrm{f}(x)\,dx = \left[\frac{2}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}} - 14x^{\frac{1}{2}}\right]_{1}^{k} = \left(\frac{2}{3}k^{\frac{3}{2}} - 14k^{\frac{1}{2}}\right) - \left(\frac{2}{3} - 14\right) = \frac{2}{3}k^{\frac{3}{2}} - 14k^{\frac{1}{2}} + \frac{40}{3}$.   [M1: limits substituted correctly]
Setting this equal to $0$ and multiplying by $\frac{3}{2}$: $k^{\frac{3}{2}} - 21k^{\frac{1}{2}} + 20 = 0$.
Let $u = \sqrt{k}$, so $k^{\frac{3}{2}} = u^{3}$: $u^{3} - 21u + 20 = 0$.   [M1: cubic in $\sqrt{k}$]
$u = 1$ is a root (when $k = 1$ the integral runs from $1$ to $1$ and is $0$; check: $1 - 21 + 20 = 0$), so $u - 1$ is a factor:
$u^{3} - 21u + 20 = (u - 1)(u^{2} + u - 20) = (u - 1)(u - 4)(u + 5)$.   [M1: factorised]
So $\sqrt{k} = 1$, $\sqrt{k} = 4$ or $\sqrt{k} = -5$.
$\sqrt{k} = -5$ is rejected because a square root is never negative (squaring it would give the false value $k = 25$, for which $\int_{1}^{25} \mathrm{f}(x)\,dx = \frac{80}{3} \ne 0$); $\sqrt{k} = 1$ is rejected because $k > 1$. Hence $\sqrt{k} = 4$ and $k = 16$.   [A1: both rejections stated]
Check: $\frac{2}{3}(16)^{\frac{3}{2}} - 14(16)^{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{128}{3} - 56 = -\frac{40}{3}$, the same as the value at $x = 1$, $\frac{2}{3} - 14 = -\frac{40}{3}$, so the integral from $1$ to $16$ is $0$.
(Meaning: $\mathrm{f}(x) < 0$ for $1 < x < 7$ and $\mathrm{f}(x) > 0$ for $x > 7$; the part of the integral below the $x$-axis from $x = 1$ to $x = 7$, equal to $\frac{40 - 28\sqrt{7}}{3}$, is exactly cancelled by the part above it from $x = 7$ to $x = 16$, equal to $\frac{28\sqrt{7} - 40}{3}$.)
question.syllabus_check: 4049 only: integration of $x^{n}$ for rational $n$ ($x^{\frac{1}{2}}$, $x^{-\frac{1}{2}}$) and a definite integral; the rewrite is splitting a fraction using the laws of indices, not substitution; the equation for the limit is a cubic in $\sqrt{k}$ solved by the factor theorem (Polynomials). No integration by substitution or by parts, no improper integral (the lower limit is $1$), no calculator needed.
question.originality_note: Written from scratch. No real 2021-2025 paper and no earlier Set asks for an unknown LIMIT of a definite integral: Set 1 P1 Q6 integrated an exponential gradient through a point and solved an exponential inequality, Set 1 P1 Q12 integrated partial fractions to $a + \ln b$, Set 1 P2 Q3 reversed a derivative to integrate $\ln(x + 1)$; GCE 2025 P2 Q3 expands an exponential product to find a curve, and GCE 2020 P2 Q7(iii) evaluates an integral with given limits that happens to be zero. Here the integrand is a quotient over $\sqrt{x}$ that must be split, and the unknown is the upper limit that makes the integral vanish, so the output of the integration becomes a cubic in $\sqrt{k}$ whose known root $\sqrt{k} = 1$ comes from the lower limit. The cubic has three distinct roots (no repeated factor, so no echo of Set 1 P1 Q12(b) or this paper's Q10), and the A1 needs a reason the candidate supplies: $\sqrt{k} = -5$ is impossible because a square root is never negative, which is the trap behind the false answer $k = 25$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both give 2/3 x^{3/2} - 14x^{1/2} + c. Checked: f(x) = x^{1/2} - 7x^{-1/2}; sympy gives the same antiderivative, 2sqrt(x)(x - 21)/3.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both k = 16. Checked: [F]_1^k = 2/3 k^{3/2} - 14k^{1/2} + 40/3 = 0 gives u^3 - 21u + 20 = (u - 1)(u - 4)(u + 5) = 0 with u = sqrt(k); u = 1 excluded by k > 1, u = -5 impossible, so k = 16. F(16) = F(1) = -40/3, so the integral from 1 to 16 is 0; the squared trap k = 25 gives 80/3. Sympy solving the integral = 0 over positive k returns only 1 and 16. The worked solution's split, (40 - 28sqrt7)/3 below the axis on [1, 7] and (28sqrt7 - 40)/3 above on [7, 16], is also right.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on both parts and both are right: (a) 2/3 x^{3/2} - 14x^{1/2} + c, (b) k = 16.
verdict.why: The round-1 fix has been made. The idea now sits in (b), where the integral's output becomes an unprinted cubic in sqrt(k). Its root sqrt(k) = 1 comes from the lower limit, and the A1 needs a reason the candidate supplies: sqrt(k) = -5 is impossible, which is the trap behind k = 25. The numbers are clean, the wording is SEAB's, and the question fits 6 marks at 1.5 minutes a mark. No 2016-2025 corpus question and no Set 1 question asks for an unknown limit (Set 1 P1 Q6 and Q12 and P2 Q3 test other integration skills). The cubic has three distinct roots, so it no longer echoes the repeated factor in Set 1 P1 Q12(b) or this paper's Q10. The session may still leave the whole question unparted as a single [6] (List B 3b/6), but that is a paper-level choice, not a flaw in this question.

question.stem: The curve $C$ has equation $y = a\cos bx + c$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are constants, $b > 0$ and $x$ is in radians. The curve passes through the origin $O$. The maximum value of $y$ is $8$ and the maximum value of $\frac{dy}{dx}$ is $24$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the value of each of the constants $a$, $b$ and $c$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: $M$ is the first maximum point of $C$ for $x > 0$. $N$ is the point on $C$ between $O$ and $M$ at which the gradient of $C$ is greatest. The tangents to $C$ at $N$ and at $M$ meet at the point $T$. Find the $x$-coordinate of $T$. Determine, with full working, whether $T$ lies to the left or to the right of $M$.
parts.answer: $x = \frac{\pi + 2}{12}$ (0.428 to 3 s.f.); $T$ lies to the left of $M$, since $\frac{\pi}{6} - \frac{\pi + 2}{12} = \frac{\pi - 2}{12} > 0$ because $\pi > 2$

question.answer: (a) $a = -4$, $b = 6$, $c = 4$ (so $y = 4 - 4\cos 6x$). (b) $x = \frac{\pi + 2}{12}$; $T$ lies to the left of $M$, since $\frac{\pi}{6} - \frac{\pi + 2}{12} = \frac{\pi - 2}{12} > 0$ because $\pi > 2$.
skills: deduce that the point of a cosine curve lying on the x-axis at x = 0 is its minimum, which forces the constant a to be negative
find b from the maximum gradient by reading the amplitude of dy/dx = -ab sin bx
meet the tangent at the steepest point of a cosine curve with the horizontal tangent at the next maximum and decide which side of the maximum they meet, by comparing (pi + 2)/12 with pi/6
question.solution:
(a) At $O$, $x = 0$ and $y = 0$: $a\cos 0 + c = 0$, so $a + c = 0$.
Since $-1 \le \cos bx \le 1$, every value of $y$ lies between $c - a$ and $c + a$, and at $x = 0$ (where $\cos bx = 1$) $y$ takes one of these two extreme values, namely $a + c$.
Here $a + c = 0$, but the maximum value of $y$ is $8$, so $a + c = 0$ must be the LEAST value of $y$: $O$ is a minimum point of $C$. Hence $a < 0$ and the maximum value of $y$ is $c - a$.
(Taking $a > 0$ would make $a + c = 0$ the maximum value of $y$, contradicting the maximum value $8$, so that case is rejected.)
$c - a = 8$ and $c + a = 0$ give $2c = 8$, so $c = 4$ and $a = -4$.
Then $y = 4 - 4\cos bx$, so $\frac{dy}{dx} = 4b\sin bx$.
Since $b > 0$, the maximum value of $\frac{dy}{dx}$ is $4b$ (when $\sin bx = 1$): $4b = 24$, so $b = 6$.
So $a = -4$, $b = 6$, $c = 4$, and $C$ is $y = 4 - 4\cos 6x$, with $\frac{dy}{dx} = 24\sin 6x$.

(b) Maximum points: $\cos 6x = -1$, so $6x = \pi, 3\pi, \ldots$; the first for $x > 0$ is $x = \frac{\pi}{6}$, where $y = 4 - 4(-1) = 8$. So $M\left(\frac{\pi}{6}, 8\right)$.
$M$ is a maximum point, so $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$ at $M$ and the tangent to $C$ at $M$ is the horizontal line $y = 8$.
Between $O$ and $M$, $0 < x < \frac{\pi}{6}$, so $0 < 6x < \pi$. The gradient $24\sin 6x$ is greatest (value $24$) when $\sin 6x = 1$, i.e. $6x = \frac{\pi}{2}$, $x = \frac{\pi}{12}$. There $y = 4 - 4\cos\frac{\pi}{2} = 4$. So $N\left(\frac{\pi}{12}, 4\right)$.
Tangent at $N$ (gradient $24$): $y - 4 = 24\left(x - \frac{\pi}{12}\right)$, i.e. $y = 24x + 4 - 2\pi$.
At $T$ this tangent meets $y = 8$: $24x + 4 - 2\pi = 8$, so $24x = 4 + 2\pi$ and $x = \frac{\pi + 2}{12}$ ($= 0.428$ to 3 s.f.). So $T\left(\frac{\pi + 2}{12}, 8\right)$.
$T$ and $M$ both lie on $y = 8$. Compare $x$-coordinates: $\frac{\pi}{6} - \frac{\pi + 2}{12} = \frac{2\pi - \pi - 2}{12} = \frac{\pi - 2}{12}$, which is positive because $\pi > 2$ (numerically $0.524 > 0.428$).
Hence $T$ lies to the left of $M$: the tangent at the steepest point $N$ reaches the level $y = 8$ before the curve does, because $C$ bends away below that tangent between $N$ and $M$. (Also $\frac{\pi + 2}{12} > \frac{\pi}{12}$, so $T$ lies between $N$ and $M$ horizontally.)

Mark scheme: (a) B1 $a + c = 0$; M1 recognising that $O$ is a minimum point (least value $0$), so $c - a = 8$; A1 $a = -4$, $c = 4$ (A0 for $a = 4$); B1 $b = 6$ from $\frac{dy}{dx} = 4b\sin bx$ with maximum value $4b = 24$. (b) M1 the tangent at $N$, using $N\left(\frac{\pi}{12}, 4\right)$ and gradient $24$, $y - 4 = 24\left(x - \frac{\pi}{12}\right)$, solved with $y = 8$ (the horizontal tangent at $M$) for the $x$-coordinate of $T$; A1 $x = \frac{\pi + 2}{12}$; B1 $T$ lies to the left of $M$, with the reason $\frac{\pi}{6} - \frac{\pi + 2}{12} = \frac{\pi - 2}{12} > 0$ because $\pi > 2$ (or $0.428 < 0.524$). A candidate who finds $x_T$ but never compares it with $x_M = \frac{\pi}{6}$ scores M1 A1 B0; a side stated without working scores B0.
question.syllabus_check: 4049 trigonometric graphs: $y = a\cos(bx) + c$ with $b$ a positive integer ($b = 6$) and $c$ an integer ($c = 4$) — greatest and least values, periodicity, the position of the first maximum; differentiation of trigonometric functions ($\frac{d}{dx}\cos bx = -b\sin bx$) and the greatest value of a sine function; the equation of a tangent to a curve at a given point, and the horizontal tangent at a maximum point. No calculator needed (an exact comparison, $\pi > 2$, closes it); nothing outside 4049.
question.originality_note: Set 1 P1 Q2 sketched a GIVEN curve y = 2 sin 3x + 1 and counted where y = k meets it; here no equation is printed, nothing is sketched and nothing is counted. Unlike GCE 2021 P1 Q7 (maximum and minimum points printed, explain c then b) and GCE 2023 P2 Q7(a) (two consecutive maxima), no turning point is stated: the candidate must decide that the origin is a MINIMUM, which forces a < 0 (a = 4 is the trap), and must get b from the maximum GRADIENT by reading the amplitude of dy/dx. Unlike GCE 2025 P1 Q12 (x-intercepts in terms of k and an equilateral triangle), the closer builds the tangent at the steepest point, meets it with the horizontal tangent at the next maximum, and decides on which side of the maximum they meet — a decision that turns on the exact comparison pi > 2, not visible from the curve's symmetry. Unlike Set 1 P1 Q13(b) (the tangent's axis intercepts, contact point shown to be their mid-point), nothing here is printed as a target and the second line is itself a tangent. Unlike GCE 2025 P1 Q10(a) (the normal to a trigonometric curve at x = 0), the point of contact is found as the greatest-gradient point, not given.

answers.(b): x-coordinate of T = (pi + 2)/12 = pi/12 + 1/6 ≈ 0.428; T lies to the left of M (M has x = pi/6 ≈ 0.524)

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both give a = -4, b = 6, c = 4. Checked: O on C gives a + c = 0. If a > 0, a + c = 0 would be the greatest value of y, which contradicts 8. So a < 0, O is a minimum and c - a = 8, which gives c = 4 and a = -4. Then dy/dx = 4b sin bx has greatest value 4b = 24, so b = 6 (b > 0 is given). C is y = 4 - 4cos 6x. A numerical scan confirms that the greatest y is 8, the greatest dy/dx is 24 and y(0) = 0.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both give x_T = (pi + 2)/12 (0.428) and put T to the left of M. Checked: M(pi/6, 8), where cos 6x = -1 first for x > 0, and the tangent there is y = 8. N(pi/12, 4), where sin 6x = 1 on 0 < x < pi/6, and the gradient there is 24. The tangent at N is y = 24x + 4 - 2pi, which meets y = 8 at x = (pi + 2)/12 = 0.4285. That is less than pi/6 = 0.5236 and greater than pi/12, so T lies between N and M, to the left of M. Confirmed numerically.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter and the blind examiner agree on every value: a = -4, b = 6, c = 4, x_T = (pi + 2)/12, with T to the left of M. My own working and a numerical check confirm the key.
fixes: Mark scheme for (b): the single A1 carries two results, x_T and the side of M, so a candidate who finds x_T but never compares it with M loses the same mark as one who fails to find x_T. Restructure the 3 marks as follows. M1: the tangent at N, using N(pi/12, 4) and gradient 24, solved with y = 8, the horizontal tangent at M. A1: x = (pi + 2)/12. B1: T is to the left of M, with the reason pi/6 - (pi + 2)/12 = (pi - 2)/12 > 0 because pi > 2 (or 0.428 < 0.524). Keep the part marks at [4, 3]: (b) sits at the top of its 3 marks but is within one mark of the work, so no re-mark is needed.

Wording of (b), light edit: 'Determine, with full working, whether T lies to the left or to the right of M.' This is the GCE 2024 P1 Q13(a) phrasing, and it means a guess read off a sketch earns nothing. The third skill phrase says the decision comes 'from pi > 2', but the scheme also accepts 0.428 < 0.524. Either add 'Without using a calculator' to (b), so the B1 really does turn on pi > 2, or reword the phrase to 'by comparing (pi + 2)/12 with pi/6'.
verdict.why: At standard. (a) carries the idea: no turning point is printed, so the candidate must decide that the origin is the MINIMUM, which gives a < 0 (the trap is a = 4), and must find b from the amplitude of dy/dx. The rebuilt (b) now turns the question round to a computed structural fact: the tangent at the steepest point meets the horizontal tangent at the next maximum between N and M, left of M. That fixes round 1's symmetry-obvious midpoint closer. It is not a re-skin of GCE 2021 P1 Q7, GCE 2025 P1 Q10 or GCE 2025 P1 Q12. It is not a repeat of Set 1 P2 Q7(a), which printed the highest point at t = 0 and the period; here the extreme at x = 0 must be deduced and b comes from the gradient. Beside Set 1's 7-mark questions (P1 Q5, P2 Q2, P2 Q5) it is as clean: two topics are bridged through the output of the first, the numbers close exactly, (b) needs (a), and the last mark is a reasoned conclusion. It stops at 4 only for the mark-scheme split and the 'with full working' edit.

question.stem: A garden is a rectangle measuring $12$ m by $5.8$ m and is enclosed by four straight walls. A lawn in the garden is in the shape of a sector $OPQ$ of a circle with centre $O$, radius $r$ m and angle $POQ = \theta$ radians. The point $O$ is a corner of the garden and the straight edge $OP$ of the lawn lies along one of the $12$ m walls. The lawn lies entirely within the garden. Edging is fixed along the straight edge $OQ$ and along the arc $PQ$ only. The total length of the edging is $15$ m and the area of the lawn is $27$ m$^2$. Find the value of $r$ and of $\theta$.
question.answer: $r = 9$, $\theta = \frac{2}{3}$ (the solution $r = 6$, $\theta = 1.5$ is rejected: the point $Q$ would be $6\sin 1.5 \approx 5.98$ m from the $12$ m wall along $OP$, more than the $5.8$ m width of the garden; for $r = 9$, $\theta = \frac{2}{3}$ it is $9\sin\frac{2}{3} \approx 5.57$ m)
skills: form a linear edging equation and a non-linear sector-area equation for a sector edged on two of its three edges, and eliminate the arc length to a quadratic in r
decide which of two positive solutions fits a rectangle: the sector's farthest point from the wall along OP is Q, at a distance r sin theta
reject the SMALLER radius because it reaches past the far wall, although both angles lie inside the right angle at the corner
question.solution:
The edging runs along $OQ$, of length $r$, and along the arc $PQ$, of length $r\theta$; there is none along $OP$, which lies against the wall.
Edging: $r + r\theta = 15$ ... (1)   [B1]
Area: $\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta = 27$, so $r(r\theta) = 54$ ... (2)   [B1]
From (1), $r\theta = 15 - r$. Substitute into (2): $r(15 - r) = 54$, so $r^2 - 15r + 54 = 0$   [M1]
$(r - 6)(r - 9) = 0$, so $r = 6$ or $r = 9$   [A1]
From (1), $\theta = \frac{15 - r}{r}$: when $r = 6$, $\theta = \frac{9}{6} = 1.5$; when $r = 9$, $\theta = \frac{6}{9} = \frac{2}{3}$   [A1]
Both angles are less than $\frac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.571$, the right angle at the corner $O$, so $OQ$ lies inside the corner in both cases; and both radii are less than $12$, so $P$ lies on the $12$ m wall in both cases. Neither pair is ruled out yet: the $5.8$ m width decides.
Take $OP$ along the $12$ m wall. Since $\theta < \frac{\pi}{2}$, a point moving along the arc from $P$ to $Q$ gets steadily farther from the wall $OP$, so the point of the lawn farthest from that wall is $Q$. With $N$ the foot of the perpendicular from $Q$ to $OP$, $QN = r\sin\theta$, and the lawn fits only if $r\sin\theta \le 5.8$.   [M1]
$r = 6$, $\theta = 1.5$: $QN = 6\sin 1.5 = 5.98$ m (3 s.f.) $> 5.8$ m, so $Q$ would lie beyond the opposite $12$ m wall. Reject.
$r = 9$, $\theta = \frac{2}{3}$: $QN = 9\sin\frac{2}{3} = 5.57$ m (3 s.f.) $< 5.8$ m, and the point of the lawn farthest along the wall $OP$ is $P$, $9$ m $< 12$ m from $O$, so the whole lawn lies within the garden.
Hence $r = 9$ and $\theta = \frac{2}{3}$.   [A1, with both distances compared with $5.8$ m]
Check: edging $9 + 9\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) = 15$ m; area $\frac{1}{2}(9^2)\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) = 27$ m$^2$.
Scheme: B1 B1 M1 A1 A1 M1 A1 = 7.
Common errors: taking the edging as the whole perimeter, $2r + r\theta = 15$, which gives $2r^2 - 15r + 54 = 0$ with discriminant $225 - 432 < 0$ and no solution; keeping both pairs because both angles are less than $\frac{\pi}{2}$; comparing $r$ itself with $5.8$ (the lawn reaches a distance $r$ from $OP$ only when $\theta \ge \frac{\pi}{2}$), which wrongly rejects both; assuming the larger lawn is the one that cannot fit.
question.syllabus_check: 4049 simultaneous equations with one linear and one non-linear equation, solved by substitution: in terms of $r$ and the arc length $s = r\theta$ the system is $r + s = 15$ (linear) and $\frac{1}{2}rs = 27$ (non-linear). Arc length $r\theta$ and sector area $\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ in radians are assumed knowledge from O-Level Mathematics (4052) and are used in 4049 radian work; the fitting condition is a sine ratio in a right-angled triangle with the angle in radians (calculator allowed, values to 3 s.f.). No vectors, statistics or other excluded content.
question.originality_note: Repaired after moderation (round 2). The earlier version was decided by the right angle at the corner alone (about 4 minutes of work for 7 marks). Now both solutions ($\theta = 1.5$ and $\frac{2}{3}$) lie inside the right angle and both radii are shorter than the 12 m wall, so the candidate must turn 'lies entirely within the garden' into a condition unaided: the farthest point of the lawn from the wall $OP$ is $Q$, at $r\sin\theta$, compared with the 5.8 m width; the smaller radius is the one rejected. No figure: a diagram would show which lawn fits.

answers.single: r = 9, θ = 2/3 (r = 6, θ = 1.5 rejected: 6 sin 1.5 ≈ 5.98 m > 5.8 m, so that lawn would not fit in the garden)

parts.label: single
parts.note: Setter and blind examiner both give r = 9, theta = 2/3, and both reject r = 6, theta = 1.5 because 6 sin 1.5 = 5.98 m > 5.8 m. I worked it too. The edging is r + r*theta = 15 and the area is (1/2)r^2*theta = 27, so r(15 - r) = 54 and r^2 - 15r + 54 = 0, giving r = 6 or 9. Then theta = 1.5 or 2/3. Check: 9 + 6 = 15 and (1/2)(81)(2/3) = 27. The orientation is forced (the lawn must open into the garden from OP), so the answer is unique.

verdict.key_verdict: No disagreement: r = 9, theta = 2/3 is right, and the smaller radius is correctly rejected on the 5.8 m width, 5.98 m against 5.57 m.

question.stem: A vertical screen is fixed to a wall. The points $B$ and $T$, on the lower edge and the upper edge of the screen respectively, lie vertically above a point $F$ on the wall, where $FB = 2$ m and $FT = 8$ m. A viewer stands in front of the wall. The viewer's eye, $E$, is at the same level as $F$, where $EF$ is perpendicular to the wall and $EF = x$ m. The angle $BET$, subtended at the viewer's eye by the screen, is $\theta$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Show that $\tan\theta = \frac{6x}{x^2 + 16}$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Given that $x$ can vary, find the value of $x$ for which $\theta$ is greatest and find this greatest value of $\theta$, in degrees. Show clearly that this is the greatest value of $\theta$.
parts.answer: $x = 4$; greatest $\theta = 36.9^\circ$ ($\tan\theta = \frac{3}{4}$); $\frac{d}{dx}(\tan\theta) = \frac{6(16 - x^2)}{(x^2 + 16)^2}$ changes from positive to negative at $x = 4$, and $\tan\theta$ increases with $\theta$ for acute $\theta$

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Show that, when $\theta$ is greatest, angle $FEB$ + angle $FET = 90^\circ$.
parts.answer: Shown: at $x = 4$, $\tan\angle FEB = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\tan\angle FET = 2$, so $\tan\angle FET = \cot\angle FEB$ and $\angle FEB + \angle FET = 90^\circ$

skills: express the angle a vertical screen subtends at the eye as a difference of two angles of elevation and simplify with tan(A - B)
maximise an acute angle through its tangent: first-derivative sign test on a rational function plus the reason that tan increases on (0, 90 degrees)
show the two angles of elevation are complementary at the best viewing distance
question.solution:
(a) $EF$ is horizontal and perpendicular to the wall and $F$, $B$, $T$ lie on a vertical line, so angle $EFB$ = angle $EFT = 90^\circ$.
Let $\beta$ = angle $FEB$ and $\alpha$ = angle $FET$ (the angles of elevation of $B$ and of $T$ from $E$).
$\tan\beta = \frac{2}{x}$, $\tan\alpha = \frac{8}{x}$.
Since $B$ lies between $F$ and $T$, $\theta = \alpha - \beta$.
$\tan\theta = \frac{\tan\alpha - \tan\beta}{1 + \tan\alpha\tan\beta} = \frac{\frac{8}{x} - \frac{2}{x}}{1 + \frac{16}{x^2}} = \frac{\frac{6}{x}}{\frac{x^2 + 16}{x^2}} = \frac{6x}{x^2 + 16}$ (shown).

(b) Let $t = \tan\theta = \frac{6x}{x^2 + 16}$, $x > 0$.
$\frac{dt}{dx} = \frac{6(x^2 + 16) - 6x(2x)}{(x^2 + 16)^2} = \frac{6(16 - x^2)}{(x^2 + 16)^2}$.
$\frac{dt}{dx} = 0 \Rightarrow x^2 = 16 \Rightarrow x = 4$ ($x = -4$ rejected since $x > 0$).
For $0 < x < 4$, $16 - x^2 > 0$, so $\frac{dt}{dx} > 0$; for $x > 4$, $16 - x^2 < 0$, so $\frac{dt}{dx} < 0$. Hence $\tan\theta$ is greatest when $x = 4$, where $\tan\theta = \frac{6(4)}{16 + 16} = \frac{3}{4}$.
$T$ is higher than $B$ and both are above eye level, so $0^\circ < \theta < 90^\circ$, and on this interval $\tan\theta$ increases as $\theta$ increases. So $\theta$ is greatest exactly when $\tan\theta$ is greatest, i.e. when $x = 4$.
Greatest $\theta = \tan^{-1}\frac{3}{4} = 36.869\ldots^\circ \approx 36.9^\circ$.
(Alternatively: $\sec^2\theta\,\frac{d\theta}{dx} = \frac{6(16 - x^2)}{(x^2 + 16)^2}$, and $\sec^2\theta > 0$, so $\frac{d\theta}{dx}$ has the same sign as $16 - x^2$: positive then negative at $x = 4$, a maximum.)

(c) When $\theta$ is greatest, $x = 4$:
$\tan\beta = \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\tan\alpha = \frac{8}{4} = 2$.
$\tan\alpha\tan\beta = 1$, so $\tan\alpha = \frac{1}{\tan\beta} = \cot\beta = \tan(90^\circ - \beta)$.
$\alpha$ and $90^\circ - \beta$ are both acute, so $\alpha = 90^\circ - \beta$, i.e. $\alpha + \beta = 90^\circ$ (shown).
[Alternative 1: $\tan(\alpha + \beta) = \frac{\tan\alpha + \tan\beta}{1 - \tan\alpha\tan\beta}$ has denominator $0$, and $0^\circ < \alpha + \beta < 180^\circ$, so $\alpha + \beta = 90^\circ$.]
[Alternative 2: $\frac{EF}{FB} = \frac{4}{2} = 2 = \frac{FT}{EF}$ and angle $EFB$ = angle $TFE = 90^\circ$, so triangles $EFB$ and $TFE$ are similar; hence angle $FEB$ = angle $FTE$, and in triangle $EFT$, angle $FET$ + angle $FTE = 90^\circ$, so $\alpha + \beta = 90^\circ$.]
Check: $\alpha - \beta = 63.43^\circ - 26.57^\circ = 36.87^\circ$, agreeing with (b).

Mark scheme guide: (a) M1 both tangents $\frac{8}{x}$, $\frac{2}{x}$; M1 $\theta$ as the difference with the $\tan(A - B)$ formula; A1 simplified to the printed result. (b) M1 differentiate $\tan\theta$ (quotient rule) and equate to 0; A1 $x = 4$; A1 $\theta = 36.9^\circ$; B1 justification: sign change of the derivative (or equivalent) AND the reason that $\tan\theta$ increases with acute $\theta$ (or the $\sec^2\theta\,\frac{d\theta}{dx}$ argument). (c) B1 $\tan\angle FEB = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\tan\angle FET = 2$ (or the ratio $2$ for similar triangles), with the conclusion and its reason (both angles acute, so they are complementary).
question.syllabus_check: 4049: addition formula tan(A - B) (trigonometric identities); quotient rule; stationary values and their nature by the first-derivative sign test; angles of elevation in a right-angled triangle. No inverse trigonometric function is differentiated: the candidate maximises tan theta and uses tan^-1 only to evaluate the final angle on a calculator. Angles are stated in degrees. Nothing outside the syllabus.
question.originality_note: Set 1 optimised volumes of solids twice (the pyramid tent with 6 m poles; the cone holding a ball) by writing a volume and differentiating it; this question optimises an ANGLE, through its tangent, with the relation built from a difference of two angles of elevation and the tan(A - B) formula, and it ends on a fact about the configuration (the two angles of elevation are complementary), not on a volume in the form k root 3. It is not GCE 2024 P1 Q3 (tan(alpha + beta) = 2 in a triangle, solved for a fixed length): here the tangent of a DIFFERENCE is built as a function of a variable distance and maximised. Not the route/time problem of GCE 2023 P2 Q9, the trough or trapezium areas of GCE 2015 P1 Q11 and GCE 2019 P2 Q11, or any box, plot or container of the exemplars. No earlier Set asked a viewing-angle or angle-subtended question.

answers.(b): x = 4; greatest θ = 36.9° (tan θ = 3/4); d(tan θ)/dx = 6(16 − x²)/(x² + 16)² is positive for x < 4 and negative for x > 4, so tan θ (and hence acute θ) is a maximum at x = 4

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both say shown. I checked it: with angle FEB = beta and angle FET = alpha, tan beta = 2/x, tan alpha = 8/x and theta = alpha - beta, because B lies between F and T. Then tan(alpha - beta) = (6/x)/(1 + 16/x^2) = 6x/(x^2 + 16). Sympy confirms the difference simplifies to 0. The target is true. The fact it turns on (theta is the difference of the two angles of elevation) is not stated in the stem, so the candidate builds the relation.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both give x = 4 and greatest theta = 36.9 degrees (tan theta = 3/4). Differentiating gives d(tan theta)/dx = -6(x - 4)(x + 4)/(x^2 + 16)^2, which changes from positive to negative at x = 4; x = -4 is rejected because x > 0. theta is acute (T is above B and both are above eye level), so the greatest tan theta gives the greatest theta. A brute-force check of atan(8/x) - atan(2/x) over 0.1 < x < 20 also peaks at x = 4.000 with theta = 36.87 degrees.

parts.label: (c)
parts.note: Both say shown. At x = 4, tan(angle FEB) = 1/2 and tan(angle FET) = 2. Their product is 1 and both angles are acute, so they add to 90 degrees; atan 2 + atan 0.5 = 90.000 degrees. The fact is general (the best distance is sqrt(FB x FT), where tan alpha tan beta = FB x FT / x^2 = 1), so the target is true by design, not by coincidence.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter and the blind examiner agree on every part, and my own working confirms the key: (a) is a true show-that, (b) is x = 4 with theta = 36.9 degrees a maximum, and (c) is true.
fixes: Re-mark: (b) gains 1 mark (3 to 4) and (c) loses 1 (2 to 1). (b) involves the quotient rule on 6x/(x^2 + 16), solving, rejecting x = -4, evaluating theta, a sign test, and the reason that tan increases on acute angles. That is more work than GCE 2024 P1 Q8(b), which paid [4] for the stationary value and nature of a cubic. (c) takes two lines once x = 4 is known: two tangents with product 1, both angles acute, so complementary. Suggested scheme at [3, 4, 1]: (b) M1 differentiate tan theta and equate to 0, A1 x = 4, A1 36.9 degrees, B1 sign change plus the monotonic reason; (c) B1 both tangents and a conclusion with its reason.

Optional: SEAB would normally print a diagram for this configuration, as GCE 2024 P1 Q3 and Q11 do. The words alone are enough to draw it (section 6 item 10), so this is not required. If a figure is added, it must not label theta as alpha - beta: that fact has to stay the candidate's.

Paper-level note for the session, not a reason to reject this slot. Max/min now appears in three questions of this paper: Q7 (greatest gradient from the amplitude of dy/dx), Q9 (this slot) and Q12 (stationary points of a rational curve). Q9 and Q12 both differentiate a rational function to locate a stationary point. Their skills differ (Q9 maximises an angle through its tangent with a first-derivative test; Q12 differentiates a partial-fraction form), so both can stand. Do not let a later re-brief add another stationary-point slot.

The A1/B1 of (b) then depends on the reason from the context (theta is acute and x > 0), which makes maximising tan theta equivalent to maximising theta, and inverse-trig derivatives are outside 4049, so the candidate must choose this route. question.stem: It is given that $\mathrm{p}(x) = x^3 + (k - 5)x^2 + (10 - 5k)x + 6k - 8$, where $k$ is a constant.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Prove that $x - 2$ is a factor of $\mathrm{p}(x)$ for all values of $k$, and that no other factor of the form $x - a$, where $a$ is a constant, has this property.
parts.answer: $\mathrm{p}(2) = 8 + 4k - 20 + 20 - 10k + 6k - 8 = 0$ for every $k$, so $x - 2$ is always a factor. $\mathrm{p}(a) = (a^3 - 5a^2 + 10a - 8) + k(a^2 - 5a + 6)$ is zero for all $k$ only if $a^2 - 5a + 6 = 0$, i.e. $a = 2$ or $a = 3$; but $\mathrm{p}(3) = 4 \ne 0$ for every $k$, so $x - 2$ is the only such factor.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the values of $k$ for which the equation $\mathrm{p}(x) = 0$ has a repeated root.

question.answer: (a) Proof: $\mathrm{p}(2) = 0$ for all $k$; $x - 3$, the only other candidate, leaves remainder $4$. (b) $k = -7$, $k = 1$ or $k = 2$
skills: prove a linear factor holds for every value of a constant by making the coefficient of k vanish, and prove no other linear factor does
repeated root of a cubic with a known factor in two cases: equal roots of the quadratic factor, or the quadratic factor sharing the known root
question.solution:
(a) $\mathrm{p}(2) = 2^3 + 4(k - 5) + 2(10 - 5k) + 6k - 8 = 8 + 4k - 20 + 20 - 10k + 6k - 8 = 0$.
The terms in $k$ cancel ($4k - 10k + 6k = 0$), so $\mathrm{p}(2) = 0$ for every value of $k$ and, by the factor theorem, $x - 2$ is a factor of $\mathrm{p}(x)$ for all values of $k$. [M1]
Collecting the terms in $k$: $\mathrm{p}(x) = (x^3 - 5x^2 + 10x - 8) + k(x^2 - 5x + 6)$.
If $x - a$ is a factor for all values of $k$, then $\mathrm{p}(a) = (a^3 - 5a^2 + 10a - 8) + k(a^2 - 5a + 6) = 0$ for every $k$. An expression $A + kB$ is zero for every value of $k$ only if $B = 0$ and $A = 0$.
$a^2 - 5a + 6 = 0 \Rightarrow (a - 2)(a - 3) = 0 \Rightarrow a = 2$ or $a = 3$. [M1]
For $a = 3$: $3^3 - 5(3^2) + 10(3) - 8 = 27 - 45 + 30 - 8 = 4 \ne 0$, so $\mathrm{p}(3) = 4$ for every value of $k$ and $x - 3$ is never a factor.
Hence $x - 2$ is the only factor of the form $x - a$ that is a factor of $\mathrm{p}(x)$ for all values of $k$. [A1]
(Alternative for the second half: a factor that works for all $k$ must work for $k = 0$, when $\mathrm{p}(x) = x^3 - 5x^2 + 10x - 8 = (x - 2)(x^2 - 3x + 4)$. The discriminant of $x^2 - 3x + 4$ is $9 - 16 = -7 < 0$, so $x^2 - 3x + 4$ has no linear factor and $x - 2$ is the only possible one. [M1 A1])
(b) Let $\mathrm{p}(x) = (x - 2)(x^2 + bx + c)$. Comparing coefficients of $x^2$: $b - 2 = k - 5 \Rightarrow b = k - 3$. Comparing constants: $-2c = 6k - 8 \Rightarrow c = 4 - 3k$. Check the coefficient of $x$: $c - 2b = 4 - 3k - 2k + 6 = 10 - 5k$.
So $\mathrm{p}(x) = (x - 2)\left(x^2 + (k - 3)x + 4 - 3k\right)$. [B1]
The equation $\mathrm{p}(x) = 0$ has a repeated root when EITHER the quadratic factor has equal roots OR $x = 2$ is also a root of the quadratic factor.
Case 1, equal roots: $(k - 3)^2 - 4(4 - 3k) = 0 \Rightarrow k^2 - 6k + 9 - 16 + 12k = 0 \Rightarrow k^2 + 6k - 7 = 0$ [M1]
$\Rightarrow (k + 7)(k - 1) = 0 \Rightarrow k = -7$ or $k = 1$. [A1]
Case 2, $x = 2$ is a root of the quadratic factor: $2^2 + 2(k - 3) + 4 - 3k = 0 \Rightarrow 2 - k = 0$ [M1]
$\Rightarrow k = 2$. [A1]
Check: $k = 1$ gives $\mathrm{p}(x) = (x - 2)(x - 1)^2$ (repeated root $1$); $k = -7$ gives $\mathrm{p}(x) = (x - 2)(x - 5)^2$ (repeated root $5$); $k = 2$ gives $\mathrm{p}(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 4 = (x - 2)^2(x + 1)$ (repeated root $2$).
The values are $k = -7$, $k = 1$ and $k = 2$. A candidate who uses only the discriminant finds $-7$ and $1$ and loses the final A1.
question.syllabus_check: 4049 polynomials: factor and remainder theorems, factorising a cubic by comparing coefficients, and the discriminant of the quadratic factor (nature of roots). The 'for all values of k' proof uses only substitution and the factor theorem; no calculus, no content outside 4049. Numbers verified by computer algebra: p(2) = 0 and p(3) = 4 identically in k; the cubic's discriminant is (k - 2)^2(k - 1)(k + 7), so the repeated-root values are exactly -7, 1 and 2, with no triple root.
question.originality_note: Set 1 P1 Q12 found k from a factor, factorised to a printed-away repeated factor and went to partial fractions; Set 1 P2 Q2 found two constants from a remainder on division by a quadratic and used a negative discriminant to show one real root. Here k stays free: the question proves a factor common to a whole family of cubics (and its uniqueness, via the coefficient of k or the case k = 0), then asks when the family has a repeated root, where the A1 hangs on keeping the second case (the quadratic factor vanishing at x = 2) that a discriminant-only answer misses. No real GCE question (two conditions for two constants then solve; GCE 2025 P1 Q3 divisibility; GCE 2013 P2 Q3 number of real roots; GCE 2006 P1 Q10 roots 1, k, k^2) has this structure; the numbers are new.

answers.(a): shown — p(2) = 8 + 4(k-5) + 2(10-5k) + 6k - 8 = 0 for all k; p(a) = k(a^2 - 5a + 6) + (a^3 - 5a^2 + 10a - 8), which is 0 for all k only if a^2 - 5a + 6 = 0 (a = 2 or 3) and a^3 - 5a^2 + 10a - 8 = 0; a = 3 gives 4 ≠ 0, so a = 2 is the only such value
answers.(b): k = -7, k = 1, k = 2  [p(x) = (x-2)(x^2 + (k-3)x + 4 - 3k); discriminant k^2 + 6k - 7 = 0 gives k = 1 or -7; quadratic has root 2 when 2 - k = 0, k = 2]

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both prove it the same way. p(2) = 8 + 4k - 20 + 20 - 10k + 6k - 8 = 0 for every k. Then p(x) = (x^3 - 5x^2 + 10x - 8) + k(x - 2)(x - 3), so p(a) = 0 for all k forces a = 2 or 3, and p(3) = 4 for every k. The alternative route through k = 0 also works: x^3 - 5x^2 + 10x - 8 = (x - 2)(x^2 - 3x + 4), and that quadratic has discriminant -7. Checked by computer algebra: p(2) = 0 and p(3) = 4 for every k.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both give k = -7, 1, 2. p(x) = (x - 2)(x^2 + (k - 3)x + 4 - 3k). The quadratic's discriminant is (k + 7)(k - 1), giving k = -7 or 1, and it has root 2 when 2 - k = 0, giving k = 2. I checked it independently: the cubic's discriminant is (k - 2)^2(k - 1)(k + 7). k = 1 gives (x - 2)(x - 1)^2, k = -7 gives (x - 2)(x - 5)^2 and k = 2 gives (x - 2)^2(x + 1). No value gives a triple root.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter and the blind examiner agree on both parts, and my own working (with computer algebra) confirms the key: (a) is a valid proof and (b) is k = -7, 1, 2.

question.stem: The diagram shows two circles, with centres $E$ and $F$, which intersect at the points $P$ and $Q$. $PA$ is a diameter of the circle with centre $E$ and $PB$ is a diameter of the circle with centre $F$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Prove that $A$, $Q$ and $B$ lie on a straight line.
parts.answer: Angle $PQA = 90^\circ$ and angle $PQB = 90^\circ$ (angles in a semicircle), so angle $AQB = 180^\circ$ and $A$, $Q$, $B$ lie on a straight line.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Prove that $EF$ is parallel to $AB$ and that $AB = 2EF$.
parts.answer: $E$ and $F$ are the midpoints of the diameters $PA$ and $PB$, so by the midpoint theorem in triangle $PAB$, $EF \parallel AB$ and $EF = \frac{1}{2}AB$, i.e. $AB = 2EF$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: The line through $P$ parallel to $EF$ meets the circle with centre $E$ again at $S$ and meets the circle with centre $F$ again at $T$. Prove that $ST = 2EF$.
parts.answer: Angles $PSA$ and $PTB$ are each $90^\circ$ (angles in semicircles), so $AS$ and $BT$ are perpendicular to $ST$; $ST \parallel EF \parallel AB$ (part (b)); so $ABTS$ is a rectangle and $ST = AB = 2EF$. (The two rectangles $SPQA$ and $PTBQ$, or the perpendiculars from $E$ and $F$ bisecting the chords $SP$ and $PT$, give the same result.)

question.answer: (a) Angles $PQA$ and $PQB$ are each $90^\circ$ (angles in semicircles), so angle $AQB = 180^\circ$. (b) Midpoint theorem in triangle $PAB$: $EF \parallel AB$, $AB = 2EF$. (c) $ABTS$ is a rectangle (angles $PSA$ and $PTB$ in semicircles, $ST \parallel AB$), so $ST = AB = 2EF$.
skills: prove three points collinear from two right angles in semicircles at a common point of two circles
midpoint theorem in the triangle formed by two diameters drawn from a common point of two circles
prove, unguided, that the chord through a common point parallel to the line of centres is twice the distance between the centres, via rectangles built from semicircle and parallel-line right angles
question.figure_description: Two intersecting circles of different sizes, drawn to scale from these coordinates (coordinates are NOT printed; no axes): Q = (0, 0) and P = (0, 4). The larger circle has centre E = (-3, 2) and radius sqrt(13) (about 3.61); the smaller circle has centre F = (2, 2) and radius sqrt(8) (about 2.83). Both circles pass through P and Q. Draw the common chord PQ as a vertical segment, P at the top and Q at the bottom. Mark the centres E (left of PQ) and F (right of PQ) with dots and draw the segment EF. Draw the diameter PA of the larger circle as a straight segment from P through E to A = (-6, 0), and the diameter PB of the smaller circle as a straight segment from P through F to B = (4, 0). Draw the straight line through P parallel to EF (horizontal), from S = (-6, 4) on the larger circle to T = (4, 4) on the smaller circle, passing through P. Label the points P, Q, A, B, E, F, S and T. Do NOT draw the segments QA, QB or AB (A, Q and B must not be joined), do NOT draw SA or TB, and do NOT mark any right angles, lengths, equal-length ticks or parallel arrows.
question.solution:
(a) Join $QA$ and $QB$. $Q$ lies on the circle with centre $E$, and $PA$ is a diameter of that circle, so angle $PQA = 90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle). $Q$ also lies on the circle with centre $F$, and $PB$ is a diameter of that circle, so angle $PQB = 90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle). $A$ and $B$ lie on opposite sides of $PQ$, so angle $AQB$ = angle $PQA$ + angle $PQB = 90^\circ + 90^\circ = 180^\circ$. Hence $A$, $Q$ and $B$ lie on a straight line. [B1 both right angles with the reason, A1 angle sum $180^\circ$ and conclusion]
(b) $E$ is the centre of the circle with diameter $PA$, so $E$ is the midpoint of $PA$ (the centre is the midpoint of a diameter). Similarly $F$ is the midpoint of $PB$. In triangle $PAB$, by the midpoint theorem, $EF$ is parallel to $AB$ and $EF = \frac{1}{2}AB$. Hence $AB = 2EF$. [B1 midpoints with reason, B1 midpoint theorem and conclusion]
(c) Angle $PSA = 90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle, $PA$ is a diameter) and angle $PTB = 90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle, $PB$ is a diameter). $S$, $P$ and $T$ lie on one straight line, so $AS$ and $BT$ are both perpendicular to $ST$, and hence $AS \parallel BT$. [B1]
$ST$ is parallel to $EF$ (given) and $EF$ is parallel to $AB$ (part (b)), so $ST$ is parallel to $AB$. [B1]
So in quadrilateral $ABTS$ both pairs of opposite sides are parallel and the angle at $S$ is $90^\circ$: $ABTS$ is a rectangle. [M1]
Hence $ST = AB$ (opposite sides of a rectangle) $= 2EF$ (part (b)). [A1]
Mark scheme for (c): any complete route earns full marks. B1 a right angle from an angle in a semicircle (or from the perpendicular from a centre to a chord) used correctly; B1 the parallel-line step ($ST \parallel AB$ from part (b), or $EF \parallel GH$ in the chord-bisector route); M1 a rectangle identified with its reason ($ABTS$, or $SPQA$ and $PTBQ$, or $EGHF$); A1 $ST = 2EF$ with the conclusion. A longer route must not be under-credited against the short one.
Alternative 1 for (c), two rectangles: from part (a), angle $PQA = 90^\circ$. Since $SP \parallel QA$, angle $SPQ = 180^\circ -$ angle $PQA = 90^\circ$ (co-interior angles), and angle $PSA = 90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle), so in quadrilateral $SPQA$, angle $SAQ = 360^\circ - 90^\circ - 90^\circ - 90^\circ = 90^\circ$ (angle sum of a quadrilateral); $SPQA$ is a rectangle and $SP = AQ$. In the same way, angle $TPQ = 90^\circ$ (co-interior angles, $PT \parallel QB$) and angle $PTB = 90^\circ$, so $PTBQ$ is a rectangle and $PT = QB$. $P$ lies between $S$ and $T$, and by part (a) $Q$ lies between $A$ and $B$ on the straight line $AQB$, so $ST = SP + PT = AQ + QB = AB = 2EF$.
Alternative 2 for (c), chord bisectors: let the perpendiculars from $E$ and $F$ to $ST$ meet it at $G$ and $H$. The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord, so $G$ is the midpoint of $SP$ and $H$ is the midpoint of $PT$. $EG$ and $FH$ are both perpendicular to $ST$ and $EF \parallel GH$, so $EGHF$ is a rectangle and $GH = EF$. Hence $ST = SP + PT = 2GP + 2PH = 2GH = 2EF$.
Check (figure coordinates): $E(-3, 2)$, $F(2, 2)$, $EF = 5$; $A(-6, 0)$, $Q(0, 0)$, $B(4, 0)$ collinear with $AB = 10$; $S(-6, 4)$, $T(4, 4)$, $ST = 10 = 2EF$. Verified numerically for general positions of $E$ and $F$ on opposite sides of $PQ$.

No tangent, no similar triangles, nothing outside 4049.

answers.(c): shown — angle PSA = 90° and angle PTB = 90° (angles in semicircles), so AS and BT are both perpendicular to ST; ST is parallel to EF, hence to AB (by (b)); so ABTS is a rectangle and ST = AB = 2EF

parts.note: Both prove it the same way: angle PQA = angle PQB = 90 degrees (angles in semicircles on the diameters PA and PB), with A and B on opposite sides of PQ, so angle AQB = 180 degrees. Correct. A and B lie on the sides of E and F because A = 2E - P and B = 2F - P.

parts.label: (b)
